## Summary

`json_sax_dom_parser::key()` copied the key from the lexer's buffer into the object. The lexer starts every token with an empty buffer (`reset()`), so the key can be moved instead. That saves an allocation and a copy for every key that does not fit into the string's inline buffer. `json_sax_dom_parser::string()` already moves string values the same way.

`ordered_map` has no rvalue `operator[]`, so `ordered_json` still copies keys. Adding one would extend a public class, so it is left out. The callback parser's `key()` is left alone too, because #5831 changes it.

This is the last of five stacked PRs from an assembly review of the number and string parsing.

## Performance

Change of the best-of-runs time against the previous PR (the first: against #5828), negative is faster. *accept* is `json::accept()` (no allocations), *parse* is `json::parse()`. Apple M1 Max: Apple Clang 21 and Homebrew GCC 16; x86-64 (Haswell VM): GCC 13, and Clang 18 with `-falign-loops=64 -falign-functions=64` on both sides (without it, code placement alone moves Clang's numbers by up to ±5 % between builds). Improvements of 3 % or more are bold.

| file | M1 Clang accept | M1 Clang parse | M1 GCC 16 accept | M1 GCC 16 parse | x86 GCC accept | x86 Clang accept |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `canada.json` | −1.4 % | +0.4 % | −1.5 % | −0.9 % | +4.0 % | −0.4 % |
| `citm_catalog.json` | +0.1 % | +0.9 % | −1.2 % | +0.0 % | −2.6 % | +0.4 % |
| `twitter.json` | +0.1 % | **−3.3 %** | +0.6 % | **−5.0 %** | +0.1 % | +0.0 % |
| `numbers.json` | +0.0 % | +0.1 % | −1.0 % | **−3.4 %** | −0.3 % | −0.1 % |
| `long_strings.json` | −1.8 % | −0.9 % | +0.0 % | +0.6 % | +0.5 % | −0.1 % |
| `twitterescaped.json` | −0.7 % | **−3.7 %** | +0.0 % | −2.5 % | −2.0 % | +0.1 % |
| `mesh.json` | −0.6 % | −2.4 % | −2.9 % | **−3.4 %** | +0.6 % | −0.3 % |

`json::accept()` builds no object, so it only shows placement noise; the gain is in `json::parse()`.


### The whole stack

All five PRs against #5828, same setup as above:

| file | M1 Clang accept | M1 Clang parse | M1 GCC 16 accept | M1 GCC 16 parse | x86 GCC accept | x86 Clang accept |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `canada.json` | **−35.1 %** | **−18.9 %** | **−32.7 %** | **−19.2 %** | **−29.0 %** | **−34.7 %** |
| `citm_catalog.json` | **−8.2 %** | −2.8 % | **−11.9 %** | **−3.6 %** | **−17.9 %** | **−5.2 %** |
| `twitter.json` | **−12.6 %** | **−9.5 %** | **−25.5 %** | **−13.6 %** | **−29.6 %** | **−14.5 %** |
| `numbers.json` | **−41.8 %** | **−37.7 %** | **−39.8 %** | **−37.5 %** | **−38.8 %** | **−39.5 %** |
| `long_strings.json` | **−27.2 %** | **−17.2 %** | **−36.4 %** | **−22.9 %** | **−46.1 %** | **−28.4 %** |
| `twitterescaped.json` | +1.3 % | **−4.1 %** | **−10.7 %** | **−8.0 %** | **−13.7 %** | +3.0 % |
| `mesh.json` | **−32.4 %** | **−14.9 %** | **−29.3 %** | **−25.1 %** | **−23.0 %** | **−32.0 %** |

Every file is faster on every build except twitterescaped.json with Clang in `accept()` (+1.3 % on M1, +3.0 % on x86-64, where the machine was under load during this run; an earlier run with aligned code on M1 measured −4.1 %). In `json::parse()`, twitterescaped.json is 4–8 % faster.

## Tests

- **New test case "object keys are moved into the value"** in `unit-class_parser.cpp`: short keys, a 100-byte key, a 16-byte key, keys with escapes, the empty key and duplicate keys. The result is compared with the byte path and with `ordered_json`, with and without `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS` / `JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS`.
- **Differential check against #5828's head** (string, `std::istream`, `FILE*`; M1 and x86-64): identical.
- **Full test suite:** passes under ASan/UBSan on macOS and Linux x86-64.
- **Fuzzing:** libFuzzer ran `fuzzer-parse_json` with ASan and UBSan for 10 minutes on the top of the stack, with four workers: about 11.5 million inputs, no findings.

## Breaking changes

None. The behavior of `json_sax_dom_parser` is the same; it only moves an argument its caller no longer uses.
